# Can County Characteristics Help Classify the 2020 Election Winner?

U.S. counties differ substantially in population size,
age composition, education, and other demographic characteristics.

In this project, we built machine-learning classifiers to predict
whether the county-level winner in the provided 2020 presidential election dataset
was Biden or Trump using county-level demographic and education information.

Rather than focusing on a single model,
we compared multiple preprocessing strategies and classification algorithms
to identify a workflow that performed consistently on unseen data.

---

## Project Overview

According to the project report,
the primary predictors included demographic and education estimates
from the U.S. Census Bureau.

One of the main challenges was the large difference
in population size across counties.

For example, a raw count of people in an age group
can be much larger in a large metropolitan county
simply because more people live there.

To make counties more comparable,
many raw population counts were converted into
**within-group or population-based proportions**.

This allowed the models to focus more on population composition
rather than county size alone.

---

## Exploring the Data

Before training the models,
we examined the distributions of the predictors.

Many of the original variables were strongly right-skewed.

Raw population counts also showed substantial scale differences across counties,
making direct comparisons difficult.

After expressing many population variables as proportions,
the predictors became more comparable across counties.

---

## No Single Predictor Was Enough

We also examined the relationship between individual predictors
and the binary election outcome.

Point-biserial correlations were calculated
between the predictors and the target variable.

No individual predictor had a correlation exceeding 0.5.

This suggested that the classification problem
was unlikely to be explained well by a single variable alone.

We therefore compared models capable of using
many predictors simultaneously.

---

## Class Imbalance

The labeled training data were not evenly distributed between the two classes.

The EDA in the report showed:

- Biden-winning counties: 389
- Trump-winning counties: 1,942

The team chose to preserve the original class distribution
rather than applying over- or undersampling.

---

## Two Preprocessing Strategies

We compared two preprocessing recipes.

### 1. Generic Recipe

The first recipe converted many population counts
into proportions based on the appropriate population or subgroup totals.

It also created growth variables for
income per capita and GDP between 2016 and 2020,
removed several identifiers and total columns,
and used median imputation for missing numeric values.

### 2. Log Recipe

The second recipe began with the Generic Recipe
and additionally applied:

- Log transformation
- Standardization

Because many predictors were right-skewed,
we tested whether these additional transformations
would improve models such as Logistic Regression and KNN.

---

## Models Compared

We evaluated three classification algorithms.

### Logistic Regression

A relatively simple classification model
that served as an interpretable baseline.

### K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

A model that classifies a new observation
based on nearby observations with similar predictor values.

### XGBoost

A boosting algorithm that builds decision trees sequentially,
with later trees attempting to correct errors made by earlier ones.

This structure allows XGBoost to capture
more complex and nonlinear patterns.

---

## Model Evaluation

We used **5-fold stratified cross-validation**
rather than relying on a single train/test split.

The training data were divided into five folds.

The model was trained on four folds and evaluated on the remaining fold,
and this process was repeated so that each fold served as the validation set.

Stratification helped maintain similar class distributions across folds.

The primary model-selection metric was **ROC-AUC**,
which measures how well a classifier separates the two classes.

---

## Model Comparison

| Workflow | Cross-Validated ROC-AUC |
|---|---:|
| Generic XGBoost | 0.973 |
| Log XGBoost | 0.973 |
| Generic KNN | 0.960 |
| Log KNN | 0.959 |
| Generic Logistic Regression | 0.959 |
| Log Logistic Regression | 0.966 |

The highest ROC-AUC was shared by
**Generic XGBoost and Log XGBoost**,
both achieving approximately **0.973**.

The additional log transformation did not improve
XGBoost performance.

The team therefore selected
**Generic XGBoost** as the final workflow
because it achieved the same performance
with the simpler preprocessing pipeline.

The selected XGBoost configuration used:

- 889 trees
- Tree depth of 4
- Minimum node size of 2

---

## Hold-Out Evaluation

After model selection,
we performed an additional 80/20 hold-out evaluation
using the labeled training dataset.

The Generic XGBoost workflow achieved
an accuracy of approximately **0.944**
on the 20% hold-out portion.

However, after refitting the workflow
on the full training dataset,
training accuracy reached **1.000**.

The gap between perfect training performance
and lower performance on unseen observations
raised a concern about potential overfitting.

---

## Looking Beyond a High Validation Score

The internal validation results were strong,
but the project also highlighted
the importance of evaluating model generalization carefully.

According to the report,
after the Kaggle private leaderboard was released,
the team's ranking fell from first to eleventh.

Although the model performed consistently
during cross-validation and the internal hold-out evaluation,
its performance did not transfer perfectly
to the hidden Kaggle test data.

This led the team to consider the sensitivity
of the model to the particular training and test samples
and the possibility of overfitting.

The report also noted that a more stable approach,
such as an ensemble of multiple models,
could be worth exploring in future work.

---

## My Role

This was a five-person team project.

According to the team-contribution record,
I worked on **Model Selection and Hyperparameter Tuning**
and also contributed to the **final report**.

I participated in comparing the cross-validation results
of Logistic Regression, KNN, and XGBoost workflows
under both preprocessing strategies,
reviewing tuning results,
and selecting the final modeling workflow.

I also contributed to interpreting the model performance
and documenting the results and limitations in the final report.

---

## What I Learned

At first,
the high ROC-AUC and hold-out accuracy
made XGBoost appear extremely robust.

However,
the perfect training accuracy
and later private-leaderboard performance
showed why a single strong metric
is not enough to evaluate a model.

The project reinforced the importance of considering
cross-validation,
hold-out performance,
training performance,
and truly unseen data together
when evaluating how well a model generalizes.

---

## Limitations

The project had several limitations.

First,
the tuning process searched only a limited grid
of 10 candidate hyperparameter configurations per workflow.

A wider search may have identified stronger settings,
particularly for XGBoost.

Second,
the final workflow was selected primarily using ROC-AUC.

The report notes that additional metrics,
such as accuracy or Brier score,
could provide a more complete evaluation.

Finally,
the perfect training accuracy
and the change in private-leaderboard performance
suggested that the final XGBoost model
required additional evaluation of its generalization ability.
